# Rotations and frames

Poses are a position plus a rotation. Reading a body pose (FK) or sending a target to IK only makes sense after you fix three conventions: **which way the axes point**, **how the rotation is stored**, and **which frame the pose is expressed in**.

## The groups $SO(3)$ and $SE(3)$

An orientation is an element of the **special orthogonal group** $SO(3)$ — the $3\times 3$ rotation matrices:

$$
SO(3) = \left\{\, R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} \;\middle|\; R^\top R = I,\ \det R = 1 \,\right\}.
$$ {#eq-so3}

The constraint $R^\top R = I$ forces the columns to be orthonormal, so lengths and angles are preserved; $\det R = +1$ rules out reflections. Rotations **compose** by multiplication ($R_1 R_2$) and invert by transpose ($R^{-1} = R^\top$) — which is why the matrix from `matrix_from_quat` is something you apply with `@` and undo with `.T`.

A full **pose** (orientation *and* position) is an element of the **special Euclidean group** $SE(3)$, written as a $4\times 4$ homogeneous transform that stacks a rotation $R \in SO(3)$ and a translation $p \in \mathbb{R}^3$:

$$
T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\[2pt] \mathbf{0}^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in SE(3),
\qquad
T\begin{bmatrix} v \\[2pt] 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Rv + p \\[2pt] 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-se3}

The homogeneous $1$ is the trick that lets one matrix **rotate and translate** a point $v$ in a single multiply (@eq-se3). Poses compose and invert in closed form:

$$
T_1 T_2 = \begin{bmatrix} R_1 R_2 & R_1 p_2 + p_1 \\[2pt] \mathbf{0}^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
T^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} R^\top & -R^\top p \\[2pt] \mathbf{0}^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-se3-inv}

Why this matters in this repo:

- Our `Pose(pos, quat)` *is* an element of $SE(3)$: `quat` is the $R \in SO(3)$ in $(w, x, y, z)$ form, `pos` is $p$. FK returns one such $T$ per body/site; the world frame is $T = I$.
- **Degrees of freedom:** $SO(3)$ has $3$, $SE(3)$ has $6$ ($3$ rotational + $3$ translational). A quaternion spends $4$ numbers on those $3$ rotational DoF under one constraint $\lVert q \rVert = 1$ — the reason $q$ and $-q$ denote the same rotation.
- **Compose, don't add:** $R_1 R_2 \in SO(3)$ but $R_1 + R_2 \notin SO(3)$ (and likewise for $T$). That is exactly why an orientation error is a geodesic, not a subtraction — the same fact behind the `q0 - q1` warning in [Rotation representations](#rotation-representations).

**Tangent space (this is what IK moves in).** For a small rotation, $R \approx I + [\omega]_\times$, where $\omega \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is an axis-angle vector and $[\cdot]_\times$ is the skew-symmetric matrix

$$
[\omega]_\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_3 & \omega_2 \\ \omega_3 & 0 & -\omega_1 \\ -\omega_2 & \omega_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad R = \exp\!\big([\omega]_\times\big).
$$ {#eq-so3-exp}

These $\omega$ (and the $6$-vector *twist* analogue for $SE(3)$) live in the Lie algebras $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and $\mathfrak{se}(3)$. That is the space a joint step $\Delta q$ pushes through: the Jacobian maps joint rates to a body twist, and `axis_angle_from_quat` is the $\log$ map (the inverse of @eq-so3-exp) that turns an orientation error into the $\omega$ our damped least-squares solver drives to zero.

## Rotation representations

All helpers in `src/robotics/math_utils.py` are batch-agnostic on the last axis. **Every quaternion in this repo is `(w, x, y, z)`** (scalar first). That matches MuJoCo `xquat`. ROS, SciPy, and many USD/Isaac stacks use **`(x, y, z, w)`**. Mixing them looks like a 90° bug, not an import error.

```python
from robotics.math_utils import quat_from_euler_xyz, quat_rotate, wxyz_to_xyzw, xyzw_to_wxyz

q = quat_from_euler_xyz(np.array([0.0, 0.0, np.pi / 2]))  # (w, x, y, z)
quat_rotate(q, np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]))                 # → +Y
# quat_rotate(wxyz_to_xyzw(q), …)  # wrong — treats x as w
```

| Representation | Shape | Pros / cons |
|---|---|---|
| Rotation matrix | `(..., 3, 3)` | Apply with `@`; 9 numbers, not unique numerically |
| Quaternion `(w, x, y, z)` | `(..., 4)` | Compose with `quat_mul`; **`q` and `-q` are the same rotation** |
| XYZ Euler (RPY) | `(..., 3)` | Human-readable yaw; gimbal lock; convention-dependent |
| Axis-angle | `(..., 3)` | Axis × radians; good for small `δR` in IK |
| Yaw only | `(...,)` | Planar base; `yaw_rotate` |

Conversions (same file): `matrix_from_quat`, `quat_from_euler_xyz` / `euler_from_quat`, `axis_angle_from_quat` / `quat_from_angle_axis`, `wxyz_to_xyzw` / `xyzw_to_wxyz`. Euler here is **intrinsic XYZ** (roll about X, then pitch Y, then yaw Z). Other libraries’ “RPY” may differ — convert through a matrix or quaternion, do not copy three floats blindly.

`wrap_to_pi` is for *angles*, not for comparing quaternions. To compare two orientations, use a geodesic (`quat_mul(quat_conjugate(q0), q1)` then `axis_angle` magnitude), not `q0 - q1`.

```bash
uv run python scripts/rotations.py
```

## Axis conventions (sim, vision, graphics) {#axis-conventions}

Most **robotics simulators** (MuJoCo, URDF/ROS, Motrix, Isaac) use a **right-handed** world frame in the same spirit as [ROS REP-103](http://wiki.ros.org/rep103):

| Axis | Typical sim / robot base |
|---|---|
| **+X** | Forward |
| **+Y** | Left (when looking along +X) |
| **+Z** | Up |

FK poses (`xpos`, `xquat`), joint axes in MJCF/URDF, and gravity (usually along **−Z**) are expressed in this frame. That is the default mental model for the rest of this tutorial.

**Vision and graphics stacks disagree.** They are still mostly right-handed, but they label axes differently — especially for **cameras**. Copying a `(3,)` position or `(4,)` quaternion from sim into OpenCV, OpenGL, or a COLMAP-style pipeline without an explicit change-of-basis looks like a small offset or a 90° “mystery rotation,” not a missing import.

| Stack | +X | +Y | +Z | Camera / viewer habit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sim / ROS-style** | Forward | Left | Up | World-fixed ground frame |
| **OpenCV** | Right in the image | Down in the image | Forward into the scene | Optical frame; “looks along **+Z**” |
| **OpenGL (classic camera)** | Right | Up | Back (toward the viewer) | Camera looks down **−Z** |

```text
  Sim world (Z-up)              OpenCV camera (common)
       +Z                              +Y ↓
        |                                |
        |                                +----→ +X
   +Y ←--+--→ +X                         /
       /                                +Z (out of lens, into scene)
     +X forward
```

**What to do at boundaries.** Whenever sim meets pixels (rendering, projection, AR, logging from a RealSense/OpenCV pipeline):

1. Name **both** frames (e.g. `world_mujoco` vs `camera_opencv`).
2. Apply one fixed **change-of-basis** rotation (matrix or quaternion) you document — e.g. “camera optical +Z aligns with robot +X when mounted forward.”
3. Convert **quaternion order** at the same time if needed (see below and [Rotation representations](#rotation-representations)).

[Never assume “right-handed ⇒ same axes.” Handedness matches; axis *labels* do not. A 4-vector from another tool is ambiguous until you know frame *and* component order.]{.common-bug-warning}

This repo’s `Pose(pos, quat)` and MuJoCo `xquat` use **sim-world axes** and **`(w, x, y, z)`** quaternions. Bridging to another stack is a small adapter (multiply by a constant rotation, swap quaternion layout with `wxyz_to_xyzw` / `xyzw_to_wxyz` in `math_utils.py`) — not a different IK problem.

### Quaternion component order (reminder)

Storage order is independent of axis convention but equally easy to get wrong:

| Source | Layout |
|---|---|
| MuJoCo `xquat`, this repo, `Pose.quat` | **`(w, x, y, z)`** — scalar first |
| ROS `geometry_msgs/Quaternion`, SciPy `Rotation.from_quat` | **`(x, y, z, w)`** — scalar last |
| USD / some game engines | Varies — read that engine’s docs |

Swapping layout without permuting components rotates about the wrong axis in practice. **Always convert explicitly**; do not reorder four floats by habit.

```python
from robotics.math_utils import wxyz_to_xyzw, xyzw_to_wxyz

q_sim = body_xquat          # (w, x, y, z) from MuJoCo
q_ros = wxyz_to_xyzw(q_sim) # safe hand-off to ROS / SciPy
```

When reading third-party poses (calibration files, SLAM, Unity/Unreal exports), check **both** the axis diagram in their docs and the quaternion order line — manufacturers rarely use the same pair as your sim.

## Link frame vs inertial frame

“Inertial” is used in two ways. Do not mix them.

**World / Newtonian inertial frame.** A frame fixed to the ground (MuJoCo’s world, `xpos` in world). Body poses from FK are usually *this* frame. Velocities may be world or body — check the API (`cvel` vs `qvel`).

**Inertial frame of a body** (COM frame). URDF `<inertial origin>` and MJCF `<inertial pos quat>` define a second frame on the *same* rigid body: origin at the center of mass, axes along principal inertia. The **link / body frame** is where the joint, geoms, and sites attach. They need not coincide.

```text
world
  └── body / link frame     ← joints, geoms, sites, FK `xpos` / `xquat`
        └── inertial frame   ← COM, `ipos` / `iquat`; MuJoCo `xipos` / `ximat`
```

Setting `pos` on a geom does **not** move the COM unless inertia is computed
`from_geom` (or you edit `<inertial>`). A mesh whose visual origin is not the COM is the usual source of “it tips over in sim.” See [Geometry and collision](geometry-and-collision.qmd#three-geometries-three-jobs) for visual vs collision vs inertial shapes. When reading poses: site/body pose is the **link** frame; if you need the COM in world, use the inertial quantities (`xipos` in MuJoCo), not `xpos`.

Motrix `Body` vs `Link` follows the same split: the rigid body (inertia) vs a kinematic frame you hang sensors and EE sites on.
